title: Review Identifies Critical Mpox Vaccine Data Gaps in Children and Pregnancy
excerpt: A scoping review reveals third-generation mpox vaccines are recommended for pregnant women and children despite an absence of direct effectiveness data in these populations.

content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 9, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Review Identifies Critical Mpox Vaccine Data Gaps in Children and Pregnancy by November 8, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Review Identifies Critical Mpox Vaccine Data Gaps in Children and Pregnancy Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Although mpox poses disproportionate risks to pregnant women and children, clinical and observational evidence on immunisation and prevention in these vulnerable groups remains limited, according to a scoping review. The researchers mapped and synthesised existing published literature on vaccines as well as non-pharmaceutical preventive measures directed at mpox in pregnant women and paediatric populations. Their investigation aimed to assess reported vaccine effectiveness and to systematically identify the critical implementation barriers and facilitators influencing real-world prevention efforts across affected healthcare settings. To conduct the synthesis, the authors executed comprehensive searches across peer-reviewed and grey literature indexed in PubMed, Scopus, and Google for records published since 2008. The team completed their final database searches on 19 September 2025. Screening and data extraction followed a pre-specified review protocol structured in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews framework. Across the evaluated literature, forty-eight peer-reviewed articles and sixteen grey literature sources met the inclusion criteria, contributing evidence on immunisation strategies, preventive measures, documented effectiveness, implementation barriers, and delivery facilitators. Within the identified literature, third-generation non-replicating vaccines, including MVA-BN, JYNNEOS, Imvanex, and IMVAMUNE, were consistently recommended for use in pregnant women and children owing to their favourable safety profiles. However, the scoping review revealed that documented observational and programmatic estimates of vaccine effectiveness were derived almost entirely from adult study populations. Reported effectiveness stood at 36 to 86 percent for a single dose and reached up to approximately 89 percent following two doses. Crucially, the review identified no effectiveness estimate specific to pregnant women or children. The authors also found that no source reported vaccine use by pregnancy trimester, paediatric data remained restricted to small studies, and recommendations for ring vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis were supported mainly by adult evidence. The review identified substantial implementation barriers that restrict mpox prevention and immunisation activities. Significant supply limitations and severe cold-chain and logistical constraints continue to impede vaccine rollout in low- and middle-income countries. In addition, vaccine hesitancy represents a major obstacle, largely driven by safety concerns that become particularly pronounced during pregnancy. These concerns are further intensified by the total absence of randomised controlled clinical trials conducted in pregnant women and paediatric groups. The authors also observed that geographic representation was severely skewed, noting that very few identified sources were centred on Africa or other low- and middle-income nations. Alongside these challenges, the scoping review documented key facilitators that have supported vaccination programs, such as international coordination, targeted surveillance initiatives, and the strategic integration of immunisation into routine maternal and child health services. The authors also highlighted flexible delivery strategies, specifically intradermal dosing, as mechanisms that can assist implementation under constrained resources. Looking ahead, the review outlined clear public health priorities, emphasising the urgent necessity of conducting prospective safety and immunogenicity studies in pregnancy and childhood, securing equitable vaccine access for low- and middle-income countries, and establishing tailored risk communication to directly address vaccine hesitancy.
